evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Quercus muehlenbergii and lists Texas in its native range.
Bell County — Fort Cavazos current INRMP identifies Chinkapin oak as a native species on the installation.
Bandera County — a documented wild Texas collection from Bandera County records Q. muehlenbergii growing naturally in canyon/creek habitat.
Real County — the USNVC Southern Edwards Plateau Bigtooth Maple Canyon Forest explicitly includes Q. muehlenbergii and is documented at several locations in Real County.
target_zone_range.guardrail: The user's single iNaturalist source-pool observation is not counted because it is not marked wild. County qualification uses explicit native/wild/ecological evidence.

morphology.look_here_first: Look at the leaf margin first: chestnut-like leaves with many regular sharp teeth, each tied to a strong nearly parallel side vein; then confirm with thin gray flaky bark and a relatively deep acorn cup.
diagnostic_traits: leaf blade obovate to elliptic, usually unlobed to shallowly undulate
roughly 8–14 pairs of strong parallel secondary veins ending in regular marginal teeth
lower leaf surface pale/glaucous with minute stellate hairs
bark light to medium gray, thin and flaky/scaly
acorn matures in one season; cup commonly encloses about one-quarter to one-half of nut

confusers.separator: Bur oak usually has much broader, deeply lobed or fiddle-shaped leaves and an enormous fringed cup; chinkapin oak has chestnut-like regularly toothed leaves without a deep midleaf waist.
White oak has obvious rounded lobes through much of the blade; chinkapin oak is primarily toothed rather than deeply lobed.
Swamp chestnut oak generally has larger leaves with coarser rounded teeth and is an East/Southeast Texas confuser rather than the typical limestone Hill Country form.
